terms.grammar: grātulor, grātulārī, grātulātus sum: with the dative of the person, and dē with the ablative, an accusative, or quod for the cause
evidence: Cic. Fam. 6.12.1: grātulor tibi, mī Balbe, vērēque grātulor
Cic. Fam. 3.12.1: ego vērō vehementer grātulor dē jūdiciō ambitūs
terms.comment: Cicero’s word; grātor is poetic and post-Augustan (Lewis & Short). Traupman’s grātulātiōnēs! (p. 295) is the English plural turned into Latin.

evidence: Verg. A. 9.641: macte novā virtūte, puer
terms.comment: Lewis & Short (s.v. mactus): applause or congratulation, “good luck! well done!”. See well done.

terms.gloss: bless it! (on news of a birth, a match, a plan)
terms.comment: The wish that answers good news; see good luck!.
Grātulātiō, a congratulating, is classical; we have found no classical instance of the plural used on its own as an exclamation. The classical way is grātulor.

phrases.latin: grātulor tibi, mī Balbe, vērēque grātulor
phrases.english: congratulations, my dear Balbus, and I mean it

phrases.latin: ego vērō vehementer grātulor dē jūdiciō ambitūs
phrases.english: I warmly congratulate you on the bribery verdict

phrases.latin: macte novā virtūte, puer, sīc ītur ad astra
phrases.english: well done, boy, on your new courage: that’s the way to the stars

phrases.latin: Puer nātus est. — Dī bene vortant!
phrases.english: A boy’s been born. — Heaven bless him!
